questions.text: Is the exposure divarasib reaches in tumour tissue the exposure that worked in the laboratory? Ask the sponsor for tumour pharmacokinetics.
Is KRAS G12C engaged in patients' tumours at the doses given? Ask for paired biopsies or circulating tumour DNA data.
What are the hazard ratios and the overall survival in the Phase 3 trial? The press release gives no numbers.
Has any other drug against KRAS failed in lung cancer for lack of efficacy? Ask a clinician who ran such trials.
Does human genetics say anything about losing KRAS function?

judgments.reason: a trial status says nothing about the size of the benefit

sentences.text: KRAS G12C is a frequent driver mutation in this lung cancer and goes with a poor prognosis, but that is association: no human genetic evidence on losing KRAS function is in the bundle.
The strongest support for the target is pharmacological: the approved G12C inhibitors already improved progression-free survival over docetaxel.
Divarasib holds the switch-II pocket in a different conformation from sotorasib and adagrasib, which is laboratory evidence of how it differs, not of benefit.
The first link is shown: divarasib binds KRAS G12C in the switch-II pocket.
Human exposure and target engagement in tumour tissue are missing links: neither is shown, and response in patients does not prove engagement.
Patient benefit rests on confirmed responses in Phase 1 and on the sponsor's report of longer progression-free and overall survival in Phase 3.

The pivotal trial is under way: a randomized Phase 3 against sotorasib or adagrasib in KRAS G12C-positive advanced non-small cell lung cancer, with progression-free survival by blinded independent central review as its primary endpoint.
The next step is the full Phase 3 readout, since the size of the benefit (hazard ratios, median progression-free and overall survival) is not in the evidence.
Patients are selected by the KRAS G12C mutation; whether a first-line trial should follow is open, because what guidelines recommend in first line is not in the evidence.
No failed program against the same target in this indication is in the bundle, so there is no failure to learn from yet.
Sotorasib and adagrasib are approved and set the bar: each improved median progression-free survival over docetaxel.
Divarasib has to beat them head to head, and the sponsor reports that its Phase 3 met its primary and key secondary endpoints.
The wider landscape (other G12C and RAS(ON) programs, other mechanisms, discontinued programs) was not searched, so competitors beyond the approved two are unknown.

The patients are those with previously treated KRAS G12C lung cancer, where the approved inhibitors add about two months of progression-free survival over docetaxel and leave room for a better option.
Whether that is commercially valuable is open: coverage, pricing against the approved inhibitors and the commercial plan are not in the evidence.
The next milestone is the full Phase 3 data; code puts the capital to reach it at $101 million (P10 $65 million, P90 $155 million) and the time at 44 months, on placeholder phase costs.
The value inflection point is the publication of the Phase 3 numbers, which the evidence does not yet give.
Roche runs the program, so its own development is the likely course; licensing or acquisition cannot be judged from public evidence.
